c: was a design style, fashion trend, and cultural movement that occurred in the 1980s and 1990s and existed until its decline in the early 2000s. This aesthetic was connected to the Pan Africanism and Afrocentric movements, which promoted racial unity across the global Black diaspora and giving African people agency over their own history through disproving and correcting Eurocentric biases in philosophy, history, and education. This aesthetic is characterized by the usage of African prints and patterns, the Pan-African colors (green, yellow, black, and red), and the centering of Black people, cultures, and stories in popular media.

Throughout the 1970s and 80s, several African countries fought for and gained freedom from their colonizing powers: Guinea-Bissau, Mozambique, Cape Verde, Angola, and Djibouti in the 70s, Zimbabwe in 1980, and Namibia in 1990. 1990 also saw the end of apartheid in South Africa, and Nelson Mandela became president of South Africa in 1994. This 30-year period was an era of revitalized Black positivity throughout the diaspora, with Afrocentrism in particular gaining most of its traction in the 80s and 90s.

This positive, pro-Black mindset was reflected in popular media, shown through a rise in diversity and representation in television and film. Aided by the Black demographic newly gaining economic power and the rise of Hip-Hop, the world began to see Black stories being told with a depth, sensitivity and respect that they hadn't been given prior. Black-led sitcoms like
The Cosby Show, A Different World, Martin

put Black narratives front-and-center in the American eye. The 80s-90s Afrocentrism aesthetic was a direct result of these things; a mixture of African political power, an Afrocentric reclamation of Black history, and a cultural shift in America towards the portrayal of Black lives in media. These things enabled this aesthetic to arise and thrive, allowing the Black community to have pride in their ethnic roots out loud, without social criticism.

This period of Afrocentrism also saw the rise of Kwanzaa as a holiday, which became widely adopted and commercialized alongside the broader Afrocentric cultural movement happening at the time. Much of the visual media of the era included Kwanzaa as a Black-focused alternative to Christmas, and educated the masses on its existence and practices.

The color palette of 80s-90s Afrocentrism is primarily taken from
the colors of the two flags that represent Pan-Africanism
: the flag of Ethiopia and the Black Liberation flag.

For the former, the colors represent development (green), hope (yellow) and the blood of Ethiopians spilled in defense from colonialism (red). These colors are common to many African national flags, borrowed from the Ethiopian flag out of respect for their triumph over colonizing powers.

For the latter, the colors represent the "the blood that unites all people of Black African ancestry, and shed for liberation" (red), "Black people whose existence as a nation is affirmed by the existence of the flag" (black), and "the abundant natural wealth of Africa" (green) as per the Universal Negro Improvement Association and African Communities League.
